remarks.text: This gives me so much joy, is my happy place in life, and I am so tortured that I only have so much time to talk about everything I’m seeing. I’m going to try to highlight master performances that have moved and inspired me and, in some cases, by a filmmaker where it’s a couple of films.
Hi, I’m Mary Bronstein. I feel like… like when I was 12 and I would go into Claire’s. That’s how I feel right now. This is so exciting.
And look, right here next to it, the lovely Ronald Bronstein, starring in Daddy Longlegs. I can’t get away from him.

Hey there, I’m Jodie Foster and I couldn’t be more excited to be in the Criterion Closet. I mean, come on, this is such an opportunity to talk about movies, my favorite thing on Earth, and just to revisit all the movies that have inspired me and that make me keep doing the same job for 60 years.

I always say that my film school was my mom. She'd pick me up from school, she'd take me to see one or two foreign films. We'd usually get food to go and then eat it in the movie theater, so that was my whole childhood, was my mom talking to me about exotic places. She really never traveled and didn't speak any other languages. That's all she ever wanted to do, was travel. So she took me to these places by showing me these movies. It's why she wanted me to speak French.

I’ve come prepared. I’m not going to give you the illusion that I’m just stumbling into the Closet like some people do, because I’m obviously a cinephile and this is a big moment for me. I did wear a Tarkovsky T-shirt. I’m not going to choose any Tarkovsky, because I’ve got all of those films.
My name is Wagner Moura. I’m an actor and director, and I’m here kind of fulfilling a dream.

[Translated] I am Jafar Panahi. I'm a movie director, an Iranian filmmaker. I was asked to come in here and take any number of films I liked. I wondered what films I should take with me. This is difficult, but the film I choose should be very important to me.
Hi, I am Lav Diaz. I am a filmmaker, a Filipino filmmaker. I’m… robbing cinema now. I’m a thief of cinema.
Hi, I’m Guillermo. I’m back in the Closet. I was the first guy to be on video and I’m super happy to be back.

And then here I’m thinking about another good friend of mine, my buddy Ted Griffin, who wrote Ocean’s Eleven and Matchstick Men. He also wrote a movie that I love called Ravenous, which… No, sorry, Ted, it’s not in the Collection. However, I did bring my own copy of Ravenous and… So Ted Griffin, Ravenous is now in the Criterion Collection. You’re welcome.

Hi, I’m Yorgos Lanthimos. It’s my second time in here and I hope I’ll do a better job this time. It’s very hard for me to talk about movies eloquently, so it’s going to be a lot of, “This is amazing.” “You have to watch this.”

But I just wanted not to tell you too many stories, but I told you three important stories. There is other directors: Guy Maddin, I work with him, I love him. I did with Isabella Rossellini movie. I do that the next time when I'm in New York, I come back.

Hello, I'm Edgar Wright and I am in the Criterion closet. I've been trying to make this happen for a number of years and it hasn't happened yet, but today, when I'm quite jet lagged, I'm going to attempt to tell you some stories about some Criterion titles, and also put them in my bag and take them home with me. This is the plan.
It’s such an honor, such an honor, Criterion. Thank you for having me. I will be back, as I make more movies, as you guys release more movies on DVD. I’m inviting myself back.
I’m going to start in this zone because these were some seminal films and some seminal ladies in my life.

Oh, yeah. So, Paper Moon, that was freaking amazing. Grifters, I remember being in the theater for that. That was a beautiful film. Oh, Crossing Delancey, that broke my heart when it came… Drugstore Cowboy. Basquiat, Jeffrey Wright. Jeffrey Wright is an unbelievable film actor. That’s a beautiful movie and a great performance. Sorcerer I discovered with my son. And there is an epic scene in that where a truck carrying dynamite is stuck on this precarious bridge. Absolutely harrowing. And Roy Scheider was absolutely brilliant in that.

Hello, my name is Nick Offerman, a sometime film actor and a great fan of the art form. And so I consider it a great privilege to be here among this Collection, with the opportunity to tell you about some of my favorite picks.
So some of the stuff that I picked are just films that bring up memories or that just remind me of a very particular time in my life, I guess.

I am a mega-collector of the Criterion Collection, so before I pick what I like to pick in my bag… here, I want to recommend a few movies that are in this part that I basically have, just to show how extraordinary is the Criterion Collection, how wide, how deep, how unapologetic and provocative in the best sense, and, ultimately, how deeply cinema it’s about.

You know, one day I was wondering, “Why am I doing this job? Is it useful?” I don’t know, I started to question. And I went to see this guy and he said, “Okay, do you like movies?” And I said, “Yes.” And he said, “Why do you watch movies? What do you feel when you watch movies? Why do you like it?” And I said, “Because I want to be moved. I want to be questioned. I want to learn things. I want to vibrate.” And he said, “Well, why do you want to vibrate? What does it… does it do to you to vibrate this way?” And I said, “Well, because I feel alive.” And he said, “Oh, you feel alive. So do you still think it’s useless what you do?” And being here, and all the emotion I’m connected with talking about those movies, reminds me every day how important art is, and movies, and I’m so happy to be part of this world.
I’m here. It’s church time. My name is Mark Duplass. I am in the Closet for the first time. My brother just got here before me, so I’m hoping I don’t pick the same movies as him.
What’s up everybody? My name is Wyclef Jean, and everybody that knows me, y’all know how I do, my whole music is all built around visuals. So today, I’m gonna pick some.

We got Boyhood. We got Blood Simple… Lone Wolf and Cub! Oh, I read a lot of those. Wow. Punch-Drunk Love. I thought I was less cultured than I think I am now. I know. I’m impressed with myself. I actually feel… I’m pretty proud of myself. I’ve seen, I’d say, a good chunk of them.
For the last one, we’re gonna pick films for each other. And the other one has to watch them. Or they’re fired.
Hello, this is Judd Apatow and I’m excited to be here in the Criterion Closet. I believe I’ve bought about 80% of these already and have watched 3% of those. I do that with books too.
And I’ll be a changed man. And I’m going to go deeper and more visual and quirkier and more cinematic with mise-en-scène. And this is going to change me.

Le cercle rouge. I love Le cercle rouge. They’ve got this amazing scene that happens in just a field. You see this car approaching, fairly ordinary car, and it just goes over this really bumpy thing to this potato field. And he gets out, smokes a cigarette, then somebody else arrives. And it’s just endlessly fascinating. You watch this thing and you can’t think, “Why am I looking at a car in a potato field?” But it’s completely brilliant.
All these are really exciting things to watch because it’s just such a… such a development in filmmaking, I suppose.
And, yeah, yo, keep making movies, keep enjoying movies, keep enjoying your life. Bong. Peace.
So, I was surprised that Psycho, my mom’s movie, was not in the Closet. Surprised, I don’t know why. But it’s not. It’s okay, Criterion.

I’ve been on the road, so I’ve been watching a lot of Criterion. Thank God for Criterion. You know, I was the one... You know, even when I was in Playboy, I was the one sitting on the ground at Samuel French reading Tennessee Williams and Eugene O’Neill and... Sam Shepard. I don’t know why, but I was. I just really wanted... Loved films and I loved theater and musical theater and movies. So, I’m so thrilled to be here and so happy to be invited here, because I don’t think people kind of expect me to be such a... Cinephile. I don’t know... I don’t know if I’m that, but I’m definitely a movie lover.

So I did one of these, these like five years ago for Hereditary, but you guys never used it because I guess I was yelling. Criterion wanted to release it now to celebrate the release of Dungeons and Dragons so, but I, I insisted that they not use the old one because there was like too much bright-eyed exuberance. Anyway, I'm gonna do it again, but I'm already regretting it because it's like, there's pressure.

Hi, I’m Ari Aster and I’m back in the Closet, this time to talk about films that have been on my mind because I’m releasing a new film, Eddington. And these are movies that belong in different traditions that Eddington could be seen as being a part of. Maybe. I hope.

Hello, I’m Bowen Yang. I’m here in the Criterion Closet or, as I’m calling it, the Prestige Pantry. I thought I was gonna come in here and be like, “I am some, like, uncultured swine. I won’t know any of this.” But this is truly, truly so breathtaking in terms of breadth, with a ‘d.’

I’m David Cronenberg, a Canadian filmmaker, born and raised in Toronto and still live there and have shot many of my films there. And in Toronto I always felt that I was halfway between Hollywood and Europe in terms of films. And when I started to make movies myself, I think that’s where I found myself, between those two poles.

By the way, I should mention that, “What’s your favorite movie?” that sort of irritates me. I mean, is there really any one movie that tops them all? I would rather people not ask me what my favorite movie is. But if you want to know, my favorite movie is The Third Man.

I guess this is sayonara. By the way, you ask people what sayonara means and they say, “Well, it’s Japanese for goodbye.” We don’t need this here, but I’m going to say it anyway. Sa-yo-nara. It’s three words. And, brace yourself, it means “if it must be so.” Isn’t that nice? See ya.
Thank you Criterion Closet for existing and the Criterion Channel and the Criterion team for keeping the art of cinema alive. You perform a vital service and we’re all very grateful.
Myself and Edgar Wright used to fly to New York sometimes just to buy Criterion DVDs from Kim’s Video. So I feel really good being here.

This was really, really fun. I watch these online because I’m a movie nerd, and to be here in this incredible library of just brilliant cinema is a real treat, so thank you very much. I’ve got some watching to do.

Movies have been the escape my whole life for me. I used to watch a lot of just horror and foreign thrillers and Japanese ’70s, like, really gory nunsploitation, the whole thing. And being in this Closet is just… it’s the most exciting part of my entire life because I feel like I can… It’s a candy shop in here.

I am going to start with Girlfriends. This film by Claudia Weill is one that I first saw, before it was so brilliantly rereleased, in a screening right after I wrote the pilot of Girls, and I thought, “Dang it, I accidentally copied this movie.” This is a incredibly moving, funny story about friendship and romance and sex and career with incredible guest appearances by such future luminaries as Christopher Guest, Bob Balaban, Melanie Mayron, all shot in ’70s New York. Favorite of Stanley Kubrick’s, who knew?
I’m just gonna say that nobody does for cinema what Criterion does. It’s a remarkable thing to be part of this collection.
To know Tariq and I, Black Thought and I, is to know that we are Criterion freaks. Let’s get started. Once the Roots’ tour bus became, like, a serious Criterion… tour bus.
I’m François Girard. I’m the director of Thirty Two Short Films About Glenn Gould. And I’m here like a kid in a candy shop, stealing the best candies there are.
When I tell you the amount of brain damage on this thing, it really is something, but the movies, I guess, I got in the bones as a youth, so they stuck there.
Hi, my name is Michelle Zauner. I play in a band called Japanese Breakfast and wrote a book called Crying in H Mart.
Oh, Double Indemnity. That is also the name of a very good porn. But I doubt that’s what that is.
[Translated] I'm thrilled to be in a place where we can dream a little more than usual. So, this is... I'm in heaven. I want to watch all these films.

[Translated] And it's true that... All my characters are people I've met in real life. All the dialogue in my films, I heard in cafés or in the street. I report on life. I film men and women that I know well. I film men and women that I'd like to have as friends, that I'd like to take in my arms. I want to make propaganda about the things I love. We live in a world that values the negative over the positive, but I'm on the positive side. Negativity is very successful, it draws big audiences. But I think everything we do in life is about loving or being loved, and all other topics are secondary. Humanity's main topic is love, in all its forms. So that's the subject that has fascinated me all my life, and in my 51 films, I've spoken about men and women... That I've loved a little more than the rest.
[Translated] And Italian cinema... I love Italy. They're French people who don't take themselves seriously, and it's great.

[Translated] I'm going to create a permanent festival for the most beautiful films in the world. In France. In Trouville. All year, we'll show the most beautiful films in the world. And these will be part of the first selection.

Uncut Gems. Wow, this movie changed my life. When Josh told me that he was going to write this movie and that he wanted me to play this part, at the time, I didn’t understand what an opportunity that would be. I think I was just like, “Okay, cool. Whatever.” Didn’t give it a second thought. And then when it all started to happen, I realized, “Oh my God.” I absolutely love this film. I would love this film even if I wasn’t in this film. It is a brilliant rollercoaster ride from hell, with really romantic, beautiful moments, heartfelt moments. I think you’re really rooting for this messed-up guy and this random girl. But yeah, I think every– I feel like everyone has watched it, but watch it again because I get residuals.
Hi, it’s Carrie Coon, finally in the Closet. Here’s the thing. This is all the old stuff. I have all of it. Because my husband is crazy.

Thank you so much. If I didn’t get to come into the Criterion Closet and get some picks, then my husband would order them and pay for them. So this has saved me a lot of money today. And I’m very grateful that you allowed me to come in. I’m so excited.

So I was going to choose Night of the Hunter, because what’s amazing about the Criterion is that it has all these extras, including an hour of dailies where you get to hear Charles Laughton direct. Sometimes I can visit set and see directors I appreciate doing their work, but to hear a master like Charles Laughton directly, his conversation with the actor, with the DP. It is the film school– That is an essential part of, I think, ever becoming a director. I would make that the lesson one and the final lesson of any school I ever had. But since I feel like I have a bunch of copies of Night of the Hunter – a lot of my DVDs do disappear because of people borrowing and not putting them back. But I’m pretty sure Night of the Hunter is still on my shelf.
It's lovely how films, when you pick up a… you have these images and memories of feelings.

I’m Brady Corbet. I’m very, very grateful to be able to do this because many years ago, seven or eight years ago, my family and I had a fire, where we lost most of our DVDs, books, and such. So, I just feel fortunate to be able to replenish the account, so to speak.
Also going to go with this new edition of Andrei Rublev, which is a film that I lost in the fire. Although I believe this is a Blu-ray.

Hi, it’s Ken Burns. I’m a documentary filmmaker. I am so happy to be locked in the Criterion Closet. My interest in film goes to my earliest days. I remember going to the movies and becoming whatever I had watched on the way home. I love that feeling, but becoming a filmmaker was born in tragedy. My mom was always dying of cancer from the time I was two or three, and she died when I was eleven. And shortly after that, my dad, who had never cried before in his life, not during her illness, not when she died, not at her impossibly sad funeral, would let me stay up late and watch films, or he’d take me out to the Cinema Guild in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and we’d look at films together of all sorts...
My name is Maura Tierney. I’m extremely excited to be here. It’s super fun. One of the funnest things I’ve done ever. Besides the Thanksgiving Parade.

I’ll have Hoop Dreams. I just watched it again recently. It’s so moving, this movie, and these kids, and the amount of time that they put into this, well, it says – it’s all the words I need – it says “revelatory.” It is.
I pick a lot of old movies– I guess I’m… I grew up in the ’70s. That’s where I sort of… It’s where my taste is drawn to.

I will recommend a film that is not here, and something that people don’t do, I don’t know if I’m allowed to do that. You have to see Le Mystère Picasso from Henri-Georges Clouzot. It’s a documentary of Picasso, about the making of... Yeah, a kind of making-of a painting of Picasso. And it’s a suspense, it’s... One of the best documentaries about creativity ever made.

name: John David Washington and Malcolm Washington

remarks.text: Basically, art is... And some great artists have said it, I mean, the great German poet and playwright and scientist Goethe said he’s only interested in works he reads that he can make use of, that he can incorporate into his own work, and isn’t that what we do? You know, you see a film and... Like I saw Antonioni’s Blow-Up and I said, “I want to make a film like that.” And so I made The Conversation. So, all of us are on the shoulders of giants. And hopefully will provide that same kind of inspiration to the, to the wonderful young people coming along. And the truth of the matter is that cinema art always changes. And, you know, the... The cinema of our grandchildren is going to be out there on the edge of almost we’re not going to be able to even understand it. It’s going to be so different. And I have a great enjoyment trying to imagine what that will be like.
[Translated] Hello, my name is Jacques Audiard. I'm a French director, and... I feel like this will all close in on me and I'll disappear, which wouldn't be such a bad fate, actually.

Hey kids, it's me, Kevin Smith, and I'm in the Criterion Closet, man. Took me a long time. 30 years to get here. Clerks was 30 years ago. It took me at least 20 seconds to reference Clerks. I like the movies that remind me of why I did it in the first place, man.

I think in coming here one thing I wanted to do is just look at titles. That’s how I got my film history. I was walking through the library after I graduated and would watch two films a day and just grab stuff that looked interesting. And boy, was that an introduction to other aesthetics.

Hello there. My name’s Jarvis Cocker. I’m here in New York. I’m short-sighted. That’s why I’m wearing these glasses. I can almost see you, but... That wasn’t diagnosed until I went to school, so I realized that, by sitting at a certain distance from the TV, I could get it in focus and see it and enjoy it. The real world wasn’t as easy as that. It was all over the place and mostly out of focus. So TV was very important to me as a kid and seemed more real than the real world in some ways, which obviously caused me some problems when I got older and had to try and live in the real world.

[Translated] This one is really great. It's a film by Sam Peckinpah, and it's considered a true classic because... I think I watched it in the 1970s, and I felt like... It's what made me fall in love with film, and sparked my desire to pursue filmmaking. It all started with this movie.

I’m Barry Sonnenfeld. I’m a film director. I used to be a cinematographer. Unfortunately, I’m not what you would call a film buff. So... And now let me turn my phone to silent. Although if someone called me, you’d get to hear Werner Herzog because I recorded Werner Herzog as my ringtone.

I now have an amazing bag of movies that I want to see again and some that I want to learn about. I love, love the Criterion Collection. So thrilled to be back here with them. They’re just a great company.

I'm Janelle Monáe, and we are in spooky season, and to be in this iconic closet is a nightmare come true. Or is it a scream come true? Hm. So I'm going to try to stay themed, guys. This is about horror, this is about Halloween, this is about the iconic films that pave the way for a lot of the new horror films that are out.
So a lot of these films that I'm going to pick, I love the music in them too.

So we are coming to an end, my time here is expiring. I just want to remind you guys that horror is a spectrum, and it's a genre that I think lends itself to talk about social commentary, to go from surrealism to a lot of dark things in a deeply comedic way. So I love the genre so much, and I'm so honored that I had an opportunity to be here in the Criterion Collection's closet. I love you.
I'm Winona Ryder, and I am so lucky to be in the Criterion closet. I basically feel like I'm at church, my church. This is like my scriptures, the scriptures I follow.

Okay, I'm going to leave, which is very difficult cuz I could literally be in here forever. But I may have to come back because word on the street is Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid is going to be in here, so it will be worth it just to come back and talk about that.

Hi, I'm Jennifer Kent, and I'm the director of The Babadook, and I'm actually here in New York City for the 10-year re-release of that film, which blows me away. What also blows me away is being in this amazing little house of art, and just having the great privilege to be able to look through these films and choose some for myself.
So I feel like I've got a lot here to take home with me, and I'm just again so thrilled to be in this beautiful space with all these filmmakers that have gone before me. It's so special.

So my name is JR. I'm an artist from France, and when I walked in here, I thought it would be my first time, but I realized that when we did Faces Places, the documentary with Agnès Varda, we actually one day came here to do some interviews. So I remember she took a little nap on one of the couch there, and so just coming here today reminding me that.

I realized that that I have so much catchup. I spend more time being in the actions of things and watching films, but when I'm on the plane, I watch films. The problem is you can't watch as DVD on the plane, so often you end up seeing things that you don't necessarily need to see. So those here, it's like a good reminder that there's a lot of things that I need to catch up.

Hi, I'm Bill Hader, and this happens to be my favorite place on Earth. Wow, this is where it all happens, huh? I went to a film school to speak, and some guy there was dressed the way I was dressed in my closet video. He came in a maroon hoodie and a House t-shirt. "This is how much I like the movie," and he went like this. So that is why I'm dressed very nondescript, because that, that, that kind of scared the out of me. No, it was very sweet. Last time I was here, it was 2009, and I said that this movie was a good date movie: Salò. "My favorite part of this movie is when and then the guy, he, he goes into a room and he finds his plate of..." It is not a good date movie, just want to clear that up. My friend Ryan Perez is this guy I worked at SNL with. He made a very good parody of these videos, like that's dead on.

The only thing I've really directed is the TV show I worked on, Barry, and the amount of knowledge I had, amount of times I would reference stuff from Criterion supplement material, I mean, it was kind of a joke.

We're so excited to be here. This is like a dream come true. I grew up in video stores, and so this is also just a nice feeling, 'cause that's not really a thing anymore, sadly. I don't get mad that I don't have late fees anymore, but okay.

It’s funny, you know, you get in here and you realize you’re influenced by so many... So many filmmakers. And they sort of... They’re etched in your head, and you’re trying to... You are this. I am this bag, you know. I bring all of this to the table when I’m directing.
I’m so good. I’m full. Thank you guys for this experience. It’s like... It’s like memory lane. It’s cathartic, too.

I have another one with me cuz I'm in New York right now, even able to come here because my new film Fancy Dance is premiering this week. And we've got one of my closest friends and greatest directors I've ever worked with just right around the corner. So Erica, would you come pick a few and teach me some new filmmakers to follow?

My name is Carol Kane. I'm an actor, and I am so moved to be in this room, this closet, with all these extraordinary films, movies—I don't know what you're supposed to call them—but all the creativity, and it's breaking my heart in a good way.

Be on these sales, I'm, I'm on these sales, I'm getting these 50% off DVDs just like, like you are, so I'm very excited to be here. Yeah, I literally, I took a picture of all my Blu-rays and my DVDs, and I made a list of all the things that I want.

I also want to say that in film school our film history class was at 9:00 a. M. On a Monday morning, which meant that all of us would immediately fall asleep the minute we got into a dark theater and like a black and white film came on, which is a horrible thing to say, but you know what, I'm in the closet, I'm telling the truth. So I'm still playing catch-up from all of those films that I unfortunately slept through because who schedules a screening at a 9:00 a. M. With a, you know, I was 18.

Hi I'm Charlie. I'm here in the Criterion Collection, which I'm very excited to be at because I've directed my first film it's called Fool's Paradise, and a lot of these films were a big influence on me.

So these are some films that were just influencing me that I managed to either work directly with the people who made them which helped me, I guess, make a movie in the tone of movies that I like but also it's just a pure joy.
Anyway, this Criterion Collection, and full of great movies. See it, come see as many of them as you can.
Now, was that as good as Ethan Hawke?

I'm Jane Schoenbrun and I'm so excited to be here and find movies. I have a lot of Criterion at home, so I got to find some new ones. Yeah, most of my disposable income goes to Criterion. I have a pitch for a movie, which is like kind of like a Detroit Rock City style one crazy night, like Orange County road trip kids try to get to the Criterion closet from the suburbs and yeah, because they all want to lose their virginity in this Criterion closet. So that's my pitch, Criterion, if you're interested.
Hey, this is Greg Gonzalez, the singer of a band called Cigarettes After Sex. Today I'm completely deep in a dream at the Criterion Closet.

I don't want to take too many things here, but just want to thank Criterion. It's the most beautiful collection in the world and deeply influential to me, and it's just been such a dream to be here just for a little bit, even. So thank you guys so much.

I'm Agnieszka Holland, and I'm following Criterion Collection from ages. I trust your choice, I trust your courage to pick the titles which are not obvious or popular, and the way you are after preparing the video is gorgeous.
It's confusing to be surrounded by so many favorites, so many friends, pals, past and present.

Film The Last Emperor here in that very beautiful Criterion Collection. Yeah, wow, I got a few of these. I won't take this one, I'll leave this for somebody else. The Double Life of Véronique, Kieślowski. I tried to make a film with him, a trilogy of films, and he was working in the same mixing studio in Paris. And one day he offered to drive me home in his car to from the studio Boulogne where we were mixing the film. He only knew one way to drive: flat on the accelerator, flat on the brake. I left the car wide. It was a very, very powerful, strong man, and we really miss him.
[Translated] When foreign films are shown in Japan, their titles are often changed, making some films difficult to recognize.
[Translated] These are films I chose. Everyone please be sure to watch them. I think you'll like them all. You won't regret it.
You guys have saved so many of these great films that would otherwise be long gone.

They all bring back wonderful memories and I'm sure that this is going to be like seeing them as they were intended by the filmmakers, which is very hard to do in a theater anymore where the films are either scratched up or with dirt all over them.

And amazingly, even some of the Blu-rays and digitals that I've seen are not as lovingly prepared as the ones that Criterion makes, most of which are in here, and to tell you the truth, most of which I have.
I guess in this little room that you call a closet is the history of world cinema and if it isn't in here it will be someday.

[Translated] In this age of subscription services, there's not all that much available from the '50s or '60s, so I'm very grateful to Criterion for their physical collection. What I'd like to introduce to you today are some Japanese films. The reason is because Japan doesn't have many '50s or '60s films on Blu-ray or DVD, so I usually buy them through Criterion and watch them. Young people in Japan haven't really seen many works by the legends from the '50s and '60s, so I'd like to introduce some of them here today.

[Translated] I'd love to show you some other Japanese films, but yes, that's nine films I've introduced today. I'd especially love it if the younger people out there go and check out these brilliant Japanese films from the '50s and '60s.

Thank you guys for having me. It was an honor to be here, paying homage to some of the most incredible directors, actors, movies. Thank you, thank you, thank you. Have a beautiful day, and if you ever see me walking around, just give me hug. Peace.
[Translated] Guillermo del Toro. The Devil's Backbone. This is my favorite of Guillermo's Spanish language films, though Pan's Labyrinth is also beautiful...
Okay, those are my movies, that's it. I'm completely and utterly never leaving my sofa. I'm going to watch them forever.
Hello, my name is Michael Cera. I'm an actor, and I'm with ICM Talent, and I'm gonna just talk about some movies that I like today.

Season seven of TCM’s podcast The Plot Thickens is all about Stanley Kubrick. More than that, the podcast is being made in conjunction with Criterion. They’re our partners on it.

name: Sharon Horgan
featured_quote: I watched it on the big screen… to say I was destroyed afterwards is an understatement. I couldn’t… I couldn’t speak.

name: Glenn Close
featured_quote: When Sidney Poitier gets back on the train and he looks back at Steiger, he smiles. And when I last saw it, I thought, 'He shouldn’t have smiled.'

remarks.text: I haven’t seen a lot of movies. There’s a big part in my life where I was basically in a cult. Not my choice. So I didn’t really go to see movies a lot.

So, there are a lot of these movies that there are… a one moment that stays with me forever. And I always kind of think that’s what art should do. It should change us. It should at least rearrange us, maybe it could be for a half an hour, it could be for a week, or it could be forever. Then there are certain images, certain scenes, certain moments in these movies that will stay with me forever.
Again, I can’t… I’m not a sophisticated cinephile, but I do have movies that I have loved. And as I said before, it’s because there are images that have stayed in my mind forever.

I’m lucky to… to have a career in film myself. I have huge respect for what it means to be a film actor. I think there’s nothing like the close-up. The only thing that has a close-up is film, because, in theater, it’s just all in long shot. But a close-up, you can see the changing of a human emotion on a face, and very powerful.

name: Aaron Sorkin
featured_quote: I was a young playwright sitting in a movie theater watching this movie and saying, ‘Jeez, I wish I had written that.’

name: Sebastian Stan

name: Zoe Kazan

remarks.text: Our films are alphabetized at home, not by number. The Criterion Collection is separate from the rest of our Blu-rays, 4Ks, and DVDs. Already we don’t have enough space, so I’m just going to make my life more difficult here.
Now I’m going to go autobiographical. These are the films that… I cannot tell the story of myself if I do not include these films. Okay. I’m going to do this chronologically in order of my life.
